"""SAE knockdown-response target specificity analysis (MaxToki-217M, block-5 TopK SAE, K562 CRISPRi).
Run from the package root. Prints all reported estimates as JSON."""
import json, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu, rankdata, hypergeom
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

SEED = 20261001
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
NPERM, NBOOT, NRAND, NPSEUDO = 10000, 5000, 1000, 200

# ---------- load ----------
npz = np.load('data/cell_feature_means.npz')
man = pd.read_csv('data/cell_manifest.csv')
pos = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(npz['rows'])}
X = npz['mean_gene'][[pos[r] for r in man['row']]].astype(np.float64)
t20 = pd.read_csv('data/feature_top20.tsv', sep='\t')
gu = pd.read_csv('data/gene_universe.tsv', sep='\t')
tr = pd.read_csv('data/targets_trrust.tsv', sep='\t')
do = pd.read_csv('data/targets_dorothea.tsv', sep='\t')
tfi = pd.read_csv('data/tf_info.tsv', sep='\t')
genes = gu.gene.values; gidx = {g: i for i, g in enumerate(genes)}
NG, F = len(genes), X.shape[1]
det = gu.detection_count.values
kdtfs = list(tfi.tf); nK = len(kdtfs)
isref = (man.group == 'ref').values; ispool = (man.group == 'pool').values; isctrl = isref | ispool

def incidence(df):
    df = df[df.gene != '<SPECIAL>']
    G = np.zeros((F, NG)); G[df.feature_id.values, [gidx[g] for g in df.gene]] = 1
    return G
G = incidence(t20)                                         # feature x gene (top-20 membership)
G_rel = incidence(t20[t20.n_active_positions >= 5])        # only top-20 entries seen at >=5 positions

# ---------- 1. responding features (KD cells vs 400 ref controls) ----------
def cohen(K, R):
    n, nr = len(K), len(R)
    sp = np.sqrt((K.var(0, ddof=1) * (n - 1) + R.var(0, ddof=1) * (nr - 1)) / (n + nr - 2))
    return (K.mean(0) - R.mean(0)) / sp

def responses(XX):
    R = XX[isref]; D = np.zeros((nK, F)); Q = np.ones((nK, F))
    for i, s in enumerate(kdtfs):
        K = XX[(man.tf == s).values]
        D[i] = cohen(K, R)
        Q[i] = multipletests(mannwhitneyu(K, R, axis=0).pvalue, method='fdr_bh')[1]
    return D, Q

D, Q = responses(X)
RESP = (Q < 0.05) & (np.abs(D) > 0.5)
nresp = RESP.sum(1)

lu = np.log(man.UMI_count.values)                          # library-size adjustment (fit in controls)
Zc = np.column_stack([np.ones(isctrl.sum()), lu[isctrl]])
B = np.linalg.lstsq(Zc, X[isctrl], rcond=None)[0]
X_umi = X - np.outer(lu, B[1])
D_umi, Q_umi = responses(X_umi)
RESP_umi = (Q_umi < 0.05) & (np.abs(D_umi) > 0.5)
del X_umi

pool_idx = np.where(ispool)[0]; sizes = tfi.n_kd_cells.values   # pseudo-knockdowns from pool controls
pseudo = []
for b in range(NPSEUDO):
    idx = rng.choice(pool_idx, rng.choice(sizes), replace=False)
    q = multipletests(mannwhitneyu(X[idx], X[isref], axis=0).pvalue, method='fdr_bh')[1]
    pseudo.append(int(((q < 0.05) & (np.abs(cohen(X[idx], X[isref])) > 0.5)).sum()))
pseudo = np.array(pseudo)

# ---------- 2. gene-level response percentiles ----------
# For KD s and gene x: mean |d| over features listing x in their top-20, ranked among genes (percentile).
# The knocked-down gene itself and every feature listing it are removed (direct CRISPRi effect, not a target effect).
def gene_pct(D, G, exclude_self=True):
    P = np.full((nK, NG), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(kdtfs):
        keep = np.ones(F, bool)
        if exclude_self and s in gidx: keep = G[:, gidx[s]] == 0
        Gs = G[keep]; A = np.abs(D[i, keep]); cnt = Gs.sum(0)
        gs = np.where(cnt > 0, (A @ Gs) / np.maximum(cnt, 1), np.nan)
        if exclude_self and s in gidx: gs[gidx[s]] = np.nan
        ok = ~np.isnan(gs); P[i, ok] = (rankdata(gs[ok]) - 0.5) / ok.sum()
    return P

P = gene_pct(D, G)
P_self = gene_pct(D, G, exclude_self=False)
self_tfs = [s for s in kdtfs if s in gidx and G[:, gidx[s]].sum() > 0]     # positive control
self_pct = np.array([P_self[kdtfs.index(s), gidx[s]] for s in self_tfs])

# ---------- 3. target sets ----------
union = pd.concat([tr[['tf', 'target']], do[['tf', 'target']]]).drop_duplicates()
SOURCES = {
    'union': union,
    'trrust': tr[['tf', 'target']].drop_duplicates(),
    'dorothea_all': do[['tf', 'target']].drop_duplicates(),
    'dorothea_ABC': do[do.confidence.str.contains('A|B|C')][['tf', 'target']].drop_duplicates(),
    'dorothea_chip': do[do.chip_flag == True][['tf', 'target']].drop_duplicates(),
}
def tset(pairs):
    return {k: np.array([gidx[g] for g in v]) for k, v in pairs.groupby('tf').target}

def boot_ci(v):
    v = np.asarray(v, float); bs = [np.nanmean(v[rng.integers(0, len(v), len(v))]) for _ in range(NBOOT)]
    return [float(np.percentile(bs, 2.5)), float(np.percentile(bs, 97.5))]

def dcenter(M):
    return M - np.nanmean(M, 1, keepdims=True) - np.nanmean(M, 0, keepdims=True) + np.nanmean(M)

# ---------- 4. matched vs mismatched TF-target pairing (primary) ----------
# M[t, s] = mean gene-level response percentile of TF t's targets in KD s.
# Specificity = diagonal of the double-centred M (own targets in own KD, beyond target-set and KD main effects).
def specificity(P, pairs, min_targets=1):
    ts = tset(pairs)
    tfl = [s for s in kdtfs if s in ts and np.sum(~np.isnan(P[kdtfs.index(s), ts[s]])) >= min_targets]
    n = len(tfl); M = np.full((n, n), np.nan)
    for c, s in enumerate(tfl):
        p = P[kdtfs.index(s)]
        for r, t in enumerate(tfl):
            v = p[ts[t]]; v = v[~np.isnan(v)]
            if len(v): M[r, c] = v.mean()
    I = np.diag(dcenter(M)); obs = float(np.nanmean(I))
    null = np.array([np.nanmean(np.diag(dcenter(M[:, rng.permutation(n)]))) for _ in range(NPERM)])
    return dict(tfs=tfl, n_tf=n, interaction=obs, ci=boot_ci(I),
                p_greater=float((np.sum(null >= obs) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)),
                p_two_sided=float((np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)),
                own_mean_pct=float(np.nanmean(np.diag(M))), own_mean_pct_ci=boot_ci(np.diag(M)),
                mismatched_mean_pct=float(np.nanmean(M[~np.eye(n, dtype=bool)])), I=I, M=M)

prim = specificity(P, SOURCES['union'])
sens = {k: specificity(P, SOURCES[k]) for k in ['trrust', 'dorothea_all', 'dorothea_ABC', 'dorothea_chip']}
sens['union_ge10targets'] = specificity(P, SOURCES['union'], min_targets=10)
sens['union_umi_adjusted'] = specificity(gene_pct(D_umi, G), SOURCES['union'])
sens['union_reliable_top20'] = specificity(gene_pct(D, G_rel), SOURCES['union'])

# ---------- 5. own targets vs detection-matched random gene sets ----------
dec = np.digitize(det, np.percentile(det, np.arange(10, 100, 10)))
ts_u = tset(SOURCES['union'])
dm = []
for s in prim['tfs']:
    p = P[kdtfs.index(s)]; tg = ts_u[s]; tg = tg[~np.isnan(p[tg])]
    obs = p[tg].mean(); ok = ~np.isnan(p); draws = np.zeros(NRAND)
    for k in np.unique(dec[tg]):
        pool = np.where(ok & (dec == k))[0]; nk = int(np.sum(dec[tg] == k))
        draws += np.array([p[rng.choice(pool, nk, replace=False)].sum() for _ in range(NRAND)])
    draws /= len(tg)
    dm.append(dict(tf=s, n=len(tg), obs=obs, pct=(np.sum(draws < obs) + 0.5 * np.sum(draws == obs)) / NRAND,
                   p=(np.sum(draws >= obs) + 1) / (NRAND + 1)))
dm = pd.DataFrame(dm); dm['q'] = multipletests(dm.p, method='fdr_bh')[1]

# ---------- 6. source-paper style: Fisher enrichment of responding features for own targets ----------
dbtfs = sorted(ts_u); sizes_db = np.array([len(ts_u[t]) for t in dbtfs])
def fisher_p(i, tg, RESPm):
    s = kdtfs[i]; keep = np.ones(F, bool)
    if s in gidx: keep = G[:, gidx[s]] == 0; tg = tg[tg != gidx[s]]
    if len(tg) == 0: return np.nan, np.nan
    link = (G[:, tg].sum(1) > 0)[keep]; r = RESPm[i, keep]
    a, K, N, n = (link & r).sum(), link.sum(), keep.sum(), r.sum()
    if n == 0 or K == 0: return np.nan, np.nan
    b, c, d_ = K - a, n - a, N - K - n + a
    return float(hypergeom.sf(a - 1, N, K, n)), float(a * d_ / (b * c)) if b * c > 0 else np.inf
fis = []
for s in prim['tfs']:
    i = kdtfs.index(s); p_own, or_own = fisher_p(i, ts_u[s], RESP)
    if np.isnan(p_own): continue
    near = np.argsort(np.abs(np.log(sizes_db / len(ts_u[s]))), kind='stable')
    comp = [t for t in np.array(dbtfs)[near] if t != s][:50]           # 50 size-matched other TFs
    pc = np.array([fisher_p(i, ts_u[t], RESP)[0] for t in comp]); pc = pc[~np.isnan(pc)]
    fis.append(dict(tf=s, nresp=int(RESP[i].sum()), p=p_own, OR=or_own,
                    pct=(np.sum(pc > p_own) + 0.5 * np.sum(pc == p_own)) / len(pc), null_rate=np.mean(pc < 0.05)))
fis = pd.DataFrame(fis); fis['q'] = multipletests(fis.p, method='fdr_bh')[1]

# ---------- 7. GATA1 ----------
gi = kdtfs.index('GATA1'); j = prim['tfs'].index('GATA1')
Xc = X[isctrl] - X[isctrl].mean(0); lc = lu[isctrl] - lu[isctrl].mean()
r_umi = (Xc * lc[:, None]).sum(0) / np.sqrt((Xc ** 2).sum(0) * (lc ** 2).sum())
gat = dict(n_resp=int(nresp[gi]), n_resp_umi_adjusted=int(RESP_umi[gi].sum()),
           umi_ratio_vs_ref=float(np.median(man.UMI_count[man.tf == 'GATA1']) / np.median(man.UMI_count[isref])),
           corr_response_vs_feature_umi_sensitivity=float(np.corrcoef(D[gi], r_umi)[0, 1]))
for k in ['union', 'trrust', 'dorothea_chip']:
    tsk = tset(SOURCES[k]); p_, o_ = fisher_p(gi, tsk['GATA1'], RESP)
    v = P[gi, tsk['GATA1']]; v = v[~np.isnan(v)]
    gat[k] = dict(n_targets=int(len(v)), fisher_OR=o_, fisher_p=p_, own_target_mean_pct=float(v.mean()))
M = prim['M']; n = len(M)
gat['all_tf_targetsets_mean_pct_in_GATA1_KD'] = float(np.nanmean(M[np.arange(n) != j, j]))
gat['GATA1_targets_mean_pct_in_other_KDs'] = float(np.nanmean(M[j, np.arange(n) != j]))
gat['interaction_union'] = float(prim['I'][j])
gat['interaction_union_umi_adjusted'] = float(sens['union_umi_adjusted']['I'][sens['union_umi_adjusted']['tfs'].index('GATA1')])
gat['detection_matched_pct'] = float(dm.set_index('tf').loc['GATA1', 'pct'])
gat['detection_matched_p'] = float(dm.set_index('tf').loc['GATA1', 'p'])
gat['fisher_pct_vs_mismatched'] = float(fis.set_index('tf').loc['GATA1', 'pct'])

# ---------- output ----------
def S(d): return {k: v for k, v in d.items() if k not in ('I', 'M', 'tfs')}
out = dict(
    n_kd_tfs=nK, n_kd_tfs_with_targets=prim['n_tf'],
    responding=dict(frac_tf_ge1=float(np.mean(nresp > 0)), frac_tf_ge1_ci=boot_ci(nresp > 0),
                    mean_n=float(nresp.mean()), mean_n_ci=boot_ci(nresp), median_n=float(np.median(nresp)),
                    frac_tf_ge1_umi=float(np.mean(RESP_umi.sum(1) > 0)), mean_n_umi=float(RESP_umi.sum(1).mean()),
                    mean_n_umi_ci=boot_ci(RESP_umi.sum(1)),
                    pseudo_frac_ge1=float(np.mean(pseudo > 0)), pseudo_frac_ge1_ci=boot_ci(pseudo > 0),
                    pseudo_mean_n=float(pseudo.mean()), pseudo_mean_n_ci=boot_ci(pseudo), pseudo_max=int(pseudo.max())),
    positive_control_kd_gene=dict(n_tf=len(self_tfs), mean_pct=float(self_pct.mean()), mean_pct_ci=boot_ci(self_pct),
                                  median_pct=float(np.median(self_pct)), frac_gt95=float(np.mean(self_pct > 0.95)),
                                  frac_gt95_ci=boot_ci(self_pct > 0.95)),
    primary_union=S(prim), sensitivity={k: S(v) for k, v in sens.items()},
    detection_matched=dict(n_tf=len(dm), mean_pct=float(dm.pct.mean()), mean_pct_ci=boot_ci(dm.pct.values),
                           frac_p05=float(np.mean(dm.p < 0.05)), frac_p05_ci=boot_ci(dm.p < 0.05),
                           n_q05=int((dm.q < 0.05).sum())),
    fisher_paper_style=dict(n_tf=len(fis), n_q05=int((fis.q < 0.05).sum()), n_p05=int((fis.p < 0.05).sum()),
                            frac_p05=float(np.mean(fis.p < 0.05)), frac_p05_ci=boot_ci(fis.p < 0.05),
                            mismatched_frac_p05=float(fis.null_rate.mean()), mismatched_frac_p05_ci=boot_ci(fis.null_rate.values),
                            mean_pct_vs_mismatched=float(fis.pct.mean()), mean_pct_vs_mismatched_ci=boot_ci(fis.pct.values)),
    gata1=gat,
)
print(json.dumps(out, indent=1, default=float))

review_generic.summary: I re-ran the full analysis script. It reproduces every number in the report and the JSON exactly, including the primary interaction of −0.0518 [−0.091, −0.013], all seven sensitivity rows, the detection-matched and Fisher summaries, and the GATA1 values. I found no coding bug. The positive control is valid: the knocked-down gene averages the 0.76 percentile in its own knockdown versus 0.50 in other knockdowns. The verdict "not supported" is defensible, because no test shows own-target specificity. However, several supporting claims are overstated or contradicted by the analyst's own outputs. (1) The power argument in the verdict ("every CI excludes even a modest fraction of the positive-control effect") is false for DoRothEA A–C. It also uses a token-removal positive control that is not on the same scale as target effects. (2) The claim that GATA1's response is "largely a library-size signature" is contradicted by the analyst's own UMI adjustment, which leaves 79% of responding features. That adjustment is also an out-of-range extrapolation. (3) The primary analysis shows a significant effect in the anti-specific direction. It is mischaracterised as not holding up in sensitivity analyses, yet the reliable-top-20 variant reproduces it. Smaller issues: an unsupported rationale for the self-exclusion step, wrong counts (8 vs 7 unmeasured TFs; 24 vs 28 TRRUST single-target TFs), missing CIs, a wrong unit on the interaction, overstated "same rule as the source paper" wording, and an overly definitive GATA1 conclusion.

points.location: Section 5 Verdict ("Every confidence interval excludes specificity of even a modest fraction of the positive-control effect"); Section 4 sentence on the +0.067 bound
points.description: The verdict's power claim is wrong as stated and rests on an invalid benchmark. (a) The DoRothEA A–C upper bound, +0.067, is 26% of the positive-control effect (+0.258), and the report itself calls this "about a quarter". So not every CI excludes a modest fraction. (b) The positive control measures removal of the knocked-down gene's own token from the input sequence (kd_remaining_frac is 0 for most TFs). Target genes instead undergo graded expression and rank changes, and the target-set score averages over up to 233 mostly D-confidence targets. A set-level interaction scaled to a single-gene token-removal effect is not a meaningful minimal detectable effect. No spike-in or power analysis was done, so how sensitive the null result is remains unknown.
points.evidence: Re-run: positive control is 0.7596 in own knockdown vs 0.5017 for the same gene in other knockdowns (difference 0.258). DoRothEA A–C CI is [−0.043, 0.067]. tf_info.tsv shows kd_remaining_frac = 0.0 for most TFs. DoRothEA confidence is 94,692 of 106,815 pairs at level D; for the knocked-down TFs it is 3,418 of 3,878 pairs.
points.recommended_action: Drop or soften the claim that every CI excludes a modest fraction. Run a power check, for example spike a realistic per-target response into a fraction of targets and see what interaction the pipeline recovers, then state the detectable effect in interpretable terms. Say explicitly that the null is limited by unknown sensitivity to graded target changes.

points.location: Section 4 GATA1 ("That response looks mostly like a library-size effect"); Section 5 Verdict ("its response is largely a library-size signature"); script section 7 / UMI adjustment block
points.description: The analyst's own UMI adjustment contradicts the library-size interpretation. GATA1 keeps 2,610 of 3,314 responding features (79%) and is still by far the largest responder. Other knockdowns lose most of theirs after adjustment: TAF5 1,623→456, GTF2B 410→19. The adjustment is also not valid for GATA1. Its cells lie mostly below the control UMI range, and they have far fewer tokens than controls, which almost all sit at the 2,048-token cap. A linear log-UMI slope fitted in controls therefore extrapolates, and after adjustment the response correlates +0.42 with UMI sensitivity, which suggests over-correction. Lower UMI and token counts may also be a biological consequence of GATA1 knockdown. The −0.71 correlation shows co-variation with UMI, not that the response is technical.
points.evidence: Re-run: GATA1 responding features 3,314 raw vs 2,610 after adjustment; mean |d| 0.84 vs 0.65. 55.8% of GATA1 cells are below the 1st percentile of control UMI (4,781). Median n_tokens is 1,780 for GATA1 vs 97.5% of ref cells at the 2,048 cap. Correlation of adjusted d with UMI sensitivity is +0.42.
points.recommended_action: Remove or soften the "largely library-size" statements. If the confound matters, model token count or truncation directly, compare against controls downsampled to GATA1-like depth, or restrict to UMI-overlapping cells. Describe the GATA1 response as partly associated with depth, without settling whether that depth change is technical or biological.

points.location: Section 4 primary analysis ("driven by TFs with only one target and does not hold up in the sensitivity analyses"); Section 6 ("unexplained"); script specificity()
points.description: The pre-specified primary test finds own targets significantly less responsive than mismatched ones: interaction CI [−0.091, −0.013], own-target mean 0.452 [0.403, 0.501] vs 0.505 mismatched. The report dismisses this. It says the effect does not hold up in sensitivity analyses, but the reliable-top-20 variant reproduces it with a CI excluding zero, and TRRUST is borderline. The attribution to single-target TFs is not computed anywhere in the script. The report also contradicts itself by calling the effect explained in Results and unexplained in Limitations. The cause is a design feature: the statistic weights 24 single-gene diagonal values equally with sets of about 200 genes, so the noisiest TFs drive the primary estimate and its CI. An unexplained, significant directional bias in the primary metric also makes its ability to detect positive specificity questionable.
points.evidence: Reliable top-20 variant: −0.046 [−0.087, −0.008], two-sided p 0.036. TRRUST: two-sided p 0.099. My subgroup check: 24 single-target TFs have mean interaction −0.115 (own percentile 0.349); 41 TFs with more than one target have −0.015 [−0.056, 0.026]; refitting on that subset alone gives −0.011, one-sided p 0.73.
points.recommended_action: Correct the sensitivity statement. Add the single-target vs multi-target breakdown to the script and report it. Consider a precision-weighted statistic or a minimum target count for the primary test. Investigate whether the anti-specific shift is a structural artefact before using the metric's null as evidence against specificity.

points.location: Section 3 Methods step 2 (self-exclusion rationale citing SMG6→UPF1 and TTF2→TSG101)
points.description: The stated reason for removing the knocked-down gene and the features that list it is that, without this, raw TRRUST pairs such as SMG6→UPF1 or TTF2→TSG101 produce spurious target signal. The data do not show this. No feature lists both genes of either pair, the own-knockdown percentiles of these targets are identical with and without the exclusion, and the primary result is essentially unchanged without it.
points.evidence: Features co-listing SMG6/UPF1 = 0 and TTF2/TSG101 = 0. P[SMG6 KD, UPF1] = 0.212 with and without exclusion; P[TTF2 KD, TSG101] = 0.050 vs 0.0499. Primary interaction without exclusion is −0.0514 [−0.089, −0.013] vs −0.0518 with it.
points.recommended_action: Remove the example or replace it with an accurate justification, for example that it avoids the knocked-down gene's own token effect, and note that the exclusion has negligible impact.

points.location: Section 6 Limitations ("Knockdown efficiency is unknown for 8 TFs whose own gene is not measured") and ("TRRUST ... 24 TFs have a single target")
points.description: Two counts are wrong. Only 7 TFs have tf_gene_measured = False. The 8th TF missing from the positive control, ZNRD1, is measured (kd_remaining_frac 0.0) but is absent from the gene universe. The "24 single-target TFs" figure is the union count; with TRRUST alone, 28 of 58 knocked-down TFs have a single target.
points.evidence: tf_info.tsv lists 7 unmeasured TFs: BRF2, FOXL2, GATA1, HINFP, HOXC10, MZF1, STAT5A. Re-run: TRRUST single-target count among knockdown TFs is 28 of 58; union count is 24.
points.recommended_action: Correct to 7 unmeasured TFs, with ZNRD1 excluded for a different reason, and give the TRRUST-specific count of 28.

points.location: Section 4 Results (several estimates); JSON estimates
points.description: The brief requires every estimate to carry uncertainty, but several reported numbers have none: the UMI-adjusted fraction of responding TFs (81.6%), the median of 24 responding features, the mismatched mean of 0.505, the positive-control median of 0.94, and the GATA1 odds ratios and percentiles. The script also computes GATA1's Fisher percentile against mismatched sets (0.82), which is not reported, even though it points in the positive direction.
points.evidence: The script output contains frac_tf_ge1_umi = 0.816 with no CI and gata1.fisher_pct_vs_mismatched = 0.82; neither has an uncertainty in the report.
points.recommended_action: Add bootstrap or exact CIs, or label the values as descriptive, and report the GATA1 mismatched-set percentile.

points.location: Section 4 GATA1 ("GATA1 is not a target-specific exception")
points.description: This is stated as a definite conclusion, but the single-TF tests have little power. With 3,314 of 4,928 features (67%) responding, the Fisher enrichment has very little room to show anything, and every GATA1 metric points weakly positive though none is significant.
points.evidence: Detection-matched percentile 0.72 (p = 0.28); Fisher percentile vs mismatched 0.82; TRRUST OR 1.21; own-target percentile 0.57 (union) and 0.61 (TRRUST).
points.recommended_action: Rephrase as "no evidence that GATA1 is a target-specific exception" and note that the tests have low power when most features respond.

points.location: Section 3 Methods step 1 ("the same rule as the source paper")
points.description: The source paper did not use the same rule. It used a Wilcoxon test of about 20 perturbed cells against 100K control token positions, with an unspecified "|effect| > 0.5", and its Fisher test looked at enrichment of the responding features' top genes. The analyst uses cell-level Mann–Whitney with Cohen's d and feature-level enrichment, so the calibration differs.
points.evidence: Source paper Section 2.9 and Methods 5.7 (pdftotext lines around 573–576 and 992–996).
points.recommended_action: Describe the rule as adapted from the source paper and list the differences.

points.location: Section 4 primary analysis ("Specificity after double-centring is −0.052 percentile points")
points.description: The unit is wrong. The value is on a 0–1 percentile scale, so −0.052 is about 5 percentile points, not 0.052 points.
points.evidence: In the script, percentiles are (rank − 0.5)/n, which lies in [0, 1]; the interaction is −0.0518.
points.recommended_action: Write "−0.052 on the 0–1 percentile scale (≈5 percentile points)".

review_checklist.summary:
I ran the analyst's full script (about 2 minutes) and it reproduces every reported number exactly: the primary interaction is -0.0518 (CI -0.091 to -0.013), the GATA1 count is 3,314 and the Fisher result is 2/48. The verdict "not supported" holds up under two stricter checks I added. Against UMI-matched control cells the union specificity is -0.030 (CI -0.076 to 0.014). Restricting targets to highly detected genes, where the positive control actually works, also gives a null result: -0.023 (CI -0.065 to 0.019) for detection > 196, and -0.003 (CI -0.022 to 0.019) for TFs with at least 10 targets.

The problems are in the claims around the verdict, not the verdict itself:
(1) The verdict overstates the test's power. It treats the positive-control effect as a yardstick, but that effect is near-total loss of the knocked-down gene and is strongly detection-dependent. It is close to chance for genes as rarely detected as typical targets. Also, the DoRothEA A–C upper bound of +0.067 is about 26% of the positive control, so not every CI excludes "a modest fraction".
(2) The linear log-UMI adjustment does not remove the library-size confound. The strongest responders are exactly the knockdowns with the lowest UMI. Against UMI-matched controls the response rate falls from 80.5% to 54% of TFs (median 24 to 2 features). Low-UMI control cells alone reproduce GATA1's response (3,027 features, profile r = 0.90).
Smaller issues: the anti-specific primary result is handled inconsistently and its explanation is not computed in the script; the bootstrap CIs are conditional on the fitted matrix; the target sets are not K562-specific (GATA1's canonical erythroid targets are absent from the gene universe); and there are a few factual or unit slips.

Checklist verdicts:
- P1: clean. Results are anchored to mismatched pairs, detection-matched sets, size-matched Fisher sets and pseudo-knockdowns.
- P2: present and unaddressed. The library-size baseline explains most of the large responses.
- P3: present, partly acknowledged.
- P4: present but acknowledged.
- P5: present and unaddressed. The library-size confound carries through the "UMI-adjusted" analyses.
- P6: present. The positive control is mechanically much stronger than any expected target effect.
- P7: acknowledged. Only block 5, one SAE and one cell line were analysed.
- P8: mostly clean. There are many sensitivity variants; only the Fisher thresholds were never swept.
- P9: present in the verdict wording.
- P10: clean, apart from one claim not computed in the script.

points.location: Results, primary analysis ('Even the most generous upper bound (+0.067) is about a quarter of the positive-control effect'); Verdict ('Every confidence interval excludes specificity of even a modest fraction of the positive-control effect'); Methods step 3
points.description: The power claim behind the null is overstated. The positive control (PC) measures the knocked-down gene's own features after that gene is almost completely removed from the cell. That is a mechanically much stronger signal than a partial expression change in a few database targets. The PC's sensitivity also depends strongly on how often the gene is detected, and is close to chance for genes at the detection level of typical targets. Specificity, by contrast, is a mean over target sets in which only some genes are plausibly regulated in K562, so any real effect would be diluted. Comparing CI bounds to a fraction of the PC is therefore not a valid statement of power. Even taken at face value, the claim is wrong for the DoRothEA A–C variant.
points.evidence:
- 59 of the 79 PC genes have kd_remaining_frac = 0 in tf_info.tsv.
- Recomputed PC percentiles correlate with gene detection count (Spearman 0.75, p = 2e-15).
- The 24 PC genes with detection ≤ 118 (the median detection of the union targets) have a mean PC percentile of 0.535. The 55 above it have 0.857.
- The PC effect against the same genes under other knockdowns is +0.258 (CI 0.19–0.32). The DoRothEA A–C upper bound of 0.067 is 26% of that, so that CI does not exclude 'a quarter'.
- The verdict still holds when targets are restricted to well-detected genes (my rerun): detection > 196 gives -0.023 (CI -0.065 to 0.019); with ≥10 targets, -0.003 (CI -0.022 to 0.019).
points.recommended_action: Remove the claim that every CI excludes a modest fraction of the PC effect. Report the PC stratified by detection. Add a power calibration, either a planted-signal simulation (shift the |d| of features linked to a chosen fraction of targets) or an explicit dilution calculation. Add the detection-restricted specificity analysis. State the null as 'no detectable specificity at the achievable sensitivity' rather than as a tight exclusion.

points.location: Methods step 1 (UMI sensitivity check); Results 'Knockdowns do change features' (UMI-adjusted 81.6%, mean 135); sensitivity table row 'UMI-adjusted responses'; GATA1 section; Verdict ('this holds across ... the UMI adjustment'); script lines lu=np.log(...) to RESP_umi
points.description: The linear log-UMI adjustment, fitted within control cells, leaves most of the library-size effect in place. The 'knockdowns clearly change SAE features' result and the UMI-adjusted robustness claims are therefore inflated. The strongest responders are exactly the knockdowns with the lowest UMI counts. The report also contradicts itself on GATA1: it calls the response mostly library size, yet its own adjustment keeps 2,610 of 3,314 responding features without comment. The specificity verdict itself survives a proper control.
points.evidence:
- The 7 knockdowns with the most responding features (GATA1, MED1, PHB2, TAF1, TAF5, MAX, RUVBL1) have the 7 lowest median-UMI ratios to ref (0.31–0.72).
- Low-UMI pool controls (n = 48, UMI ≤ GATA1's 90th percentile) compared with ref give 3,027 responding features. Their effect-size profile correlates r = 0.90 with GATA1's.
- GATA1 against UMI-matched controls gives 1,311 responding features (linear adjustment: 2,610).
- Other knockdowns, ref vs UMI-matched: MED1 2,551 vs 176; TAF1 1,968 vs 128; PHB2 2,192 vs 372; MAX 1,623 vs 180.
- Across all 87 TFs, UMI-matched controls give 54% of TFs with ≥1 responding feature (median 2), versus the reported 80.5% (median 24) and 81.6% after adjustment. Matched controls have smaller n, so this needs its own pseudo-knockdown calibration.
- Specificity with UMI-matched controls stays null: union -0.030 (CI -0.076 to 0.014); ≥10 targets -0.009 (CI -0.018 to 0.001).
points.recommended_action: Replace or supplement the linear adjustment with UMI-matched (or n_tokens-matched) control comparisons, calibrated by pseudo-knockdowns drawn in the same matched design. Restate the response-rate headline under that control. Report the low-UMI-control result as the evidence for the GATA1 library-size interpretation, and explain why the linear adjustment under-corrects (GATA1 cells sit at the low edge of the control UMI range, and ref cells sit at the 2,048-token cap).

points.location: Results, primary analysis ('That opposite effect is driven by TFs with only one target and does not hold up in the sensitivity analyses'); Limitations ('The small anti-specific estimate ... is unexplained'); analysis_script
points.description: The significant anti-specific primary estimate is handled inconsistently. The claim that it does not hold up in the sensitivity analyses is partly false: the reliable-top-20 variant also has a CI excluding zero. The attribution to single-target TFs is correct, but the script never computes it, so it is not reproducible from the deliverable. The Limitations section then calls the estimate unexplained, which contradicts the Results.
points.evidence:
- Reliable-top-20 variant: -0.046 (CI -0.087 to -0.008); two-sided permutation p = 0.036 from the analyst's own script output.
- My breakdown of the primary interaction: the 24 single-target TFs have mean -0.115 (CI -0.18 to -0.04). Refitting on TFs with ≥2 targets gives -0.011 (CI -0.049 to 0.028).
- Neither number appears in the analysis_script.
points.recommended_action: Add the breakdown by target-set size to the script and the results. Note that the reliable-top-20 variant also excludes zero. Make the Results and Limitations wording consistent.

points.location: Methods step 4 / Results (all specificity CIs); script boot_ci(I)
points.description: The specificity CIs come from resampling the per-TF diagonal values of a single fitted, double-centred matrix. Cell-level sampling error in the effect sizes is not propagated, and the double-centring makes the diagonal values dependent on each other, so the CIs are probably too narrow. The verdict's exclusion language relies on these upper bounds. The limitation is acknowledged.
points.evidence:
- boot_ci(I) resamples I = diag(dcenter(M)) with M fixed.
- The same CIs are used to state that the primary estimate excludes zero (-0.091 to -0.013) and to bound specificity in the verdict.
points.recommended_action: Use a hierarchical bootstrap: resample cells within each knockdown and within ref, recompute effect sizes, percentiles and the matrix, then resample TFs. Alternatively, base inference on the permutation p-values and present the CIs as approximate.

points.location: Data / Limitations (target databases); GATA1 section ('GATA1 is not a target-specific exception')
points.description: Endpoint mismatch: the target sets are not specific to K562, and this is not stated. GATA1's canonical erythroid targets in K562 are missing from the gene universe entirely, so the GATA1 conclusion only covers non-canonical database targets. Many of the 87 knocked-down 'TFs' are not sequence-specific TFs and have a single literature-derived target, yet they make up 24 of the 65 TFs in the primary analysis.
points.evidence:
- None of HBG1, HBG2, HBA1, HBZ, GYPA, ALAS2, KLF1, TAL1, EPOR, NFE2, LMO2, GATA2 or MYB is in gene_universe.tsv.
- GATA1's 11 TRRUST targets in the universe are AGGF1, BACH1, CBFB, CDC6, COPS5, DICER1, DPYSL2, GNAS, RUNX1, SMAD1 and ZNF268.
- Single-target 'TFs' include ENO1, MCM2, MCM5, RAD51, SMG6, TTF2, UPF2 and PHB2. Union target sets are dominated by DoRothEA level D (94,692 of 106,815 pairs).
points.recommended_action: State that the target sets come from curated or inferred sources not specific to K562, and that GATA1's canonical K562 targets cannot be tested with this gene universe. Limit the GATA1 conclusion accordingly. Consider a sensitivity analysis restricted to sequence-specific TFs.

points.location: Limitations ('Knockdown efficiency is unknown for 8 TFs'; 'TRRUST gives very small sets here (24 TFs have a single target)'); Results ('−0.052 percentile points')
points.description: Several factual or unit errors.
points.evidence:
- tf_info.tsv lists 7 TFs whose gene is not measured, not 8: BRF2, FOXL2, GATA1, HINFP, HOXC10, MZF1, STAT5A.
- 24 single-target TFs is the union count. For TRRUST alone it is 28 of 58 TFs.
- The specificity is -0.052 on a 0–1 percentile scale, which is -5.2 percentile points, not -0.052 points.
points.recommended_action: Correct the counts and attribute each one to the right target source. Express specificity either as a fraction on the 0–1 scale or as percentile points (×100).

points.location: Methods step 6 / Results 'Source-paper style Fisher test'
points.description: The 'source-paper style' test is not a like-for-like replication, and it uses a single threshold. The source paper tested TRRUST targets, while the deliverable uses union targets, so it is not directly comparable to the paper's 3/48. The responding-feature rule (FDR < 0.05, |d| > 0.5) is never varied for this thresholded test.
points.evidence:
- The source paper (Section 2.9) tests 'each TRRUST TF'.
- The script calls fisher_p with ts_u (union targets) for all TFs; TRRUST is used only for GATA1.
- No threshold sweep appears anywhere in the script.
points.recommended_action: Add a Fisher run with TRRUST-only targets for comparability with the paper. Add a 3-point sweep over the |d| or FDR threshold and report the worst case.

repaired_generic.report:
# SAE knockdown responses and TF target genes (MaxToki-217M, block-5 TopK SAE, K562 CRISPRi)

## 1. Question
When a transcription factor (TF) is knocked down, do the SAE features that respond pick out that TF's own target genes more than they pick out other genes? The question covers all knocked-down TFs. GATA1 is looked at separately. The verdict is one of supported, not supported or inconclusive.

## 2. Data
All files come from `data/`:
- **`cell_feature_means.npz`**: per-cell mean activation of each of the 4,928 features for 9,200 cells, plus token counts. Rows were matched to the manifest by cell id.
- **`cell_manifest.csv`**:
  - `kd`: 7,500 cells covering 87 TFs.
  - `ref`: 400 control cells, the comparison group.
  - `pool`: 800 control cells, used for pseudo-knockdowns and as depth-matched controls.
  - `catalog`: the SAE training cells, not used as controls.
  - UMI counts were used for the library-size analyses.
- **`feature_top20.tsv`**: links each feature to genes through its top-20 list. The `<SPECIAL>` token was dropped. 17% of entries were seen at only one position.
- **`gene_universe.tsv`**: 6,324 genes, with detection counts used to build matched null gene sets.
- **`targets_trrust.tsv`** and **`targets_dorothea.tsv`**: the primary analysis uses the union of the two (621 database TFs). Sensitivity analyses use TRRUST only, DoRothEA all levels, DoRothEA A–C and DoRothEA ChIP-flagged pairs. DoRothEA is dominated by confidence level D: 94,692 of 106,815 pairs, and 3,418 of 3,878 pairs for the knocked-down TFs.
- **`tf_info.tsv`**: knockdown group sizes and remaining TF mRNA. For 7 TFs the TF's own gene is not measured (BRF2, FOXL2, GATA1, HINFP, HOXC10, MZF1, STAT5A). For 60 of the 80 measured TFs, no TF mRNA remains (the largest remaining fraction is 0.13).

**Target coverage.**
- 65 of the 87 TFs have at least one union target in the gene universe. 24 of these 65 have exactly one target, 22 have at least 10, and the largest set has 298.
- With TRRUST alone, 28 of 58 TFs have a single target.
- 79 TFs have their own gene in the universe and enter the positive control. The 8 excluded are the 7 unmeasured TFs plus ZNRD1, which is measured but is not in the gene universe.

## 3. Methods
1. **Which features respond.** The rule is adapted from the source paper, not the same as it.
   - The paper tested about 20 perturbed cells against 100K control token positions with a Wilcoxon test (BH FDR < 0.05, |effect| > 0.5, effect measure not specified).
   - Here, all knockdown cells of a TF (34–100) were compared with the 400 `ref` cells at the cell level, feature by feature. I used a Mann–Whitney test, BH correction across the 4,928 features, and Cohen's d as the effect size. A feature "responds" if FDR < 0.05 and |d| > 0.5.
   - The unit, sample sizes and effect measure differ from the paper, so I calibrated the rule directly. I drew 200 pseudo-knockdowns of random `pool` cells (sizes drawn from the real knockdown group sizes) and tested them against `ref`.
   - Sensitivity check: the same test after regressing each feature on log(UMI) within control cells (linear library-size adjustment).
2. **Gene-level response score.**
   - For knockdown s and gene x, I took the mean |d| over the features whose top-20 list contains x, and converted it to a percentile rank among genes (0–1 scale).
   - The knocked-down gene itself, and every feature that lists it, were removed before ranking. This keeps the direct CRISPRi effect on the knocked-down gene's own token, which is large (step 3), out of target scores.
   - In practice the exclusion changes almost nothing; this was checked by re-running without it.
3. **Positive control.**
   - I took the percentile of the knocked-down gene itself in its own knockdown (without the exclusion) and compared it with the same gene in the other 86 knockdowns. I also measured the shift in mean |d| of the features that list the gene.
   - Most knocked-down TFs lose essentially all their mRNA, so this mostly measures the loss of the gene's token from the cell's input.
   - It shows that the pipeline can see a gene-specific change at all. It is not a benchmark for graded target changes; step 6 addresses that.
4. **Primary specificity test (pre-specified).**
   - M[t, s] is the mean response percentile of TF t's targets under the knockdown of TF s, over the 65 TFs with targets.
   - Double-centring removes the row effect (how responsive a target set is in general) and the column effect (how strong a knockdown is overall). What is left on the diagonal is "own targets in own knockdown" beyond these two effects.
   - The statistic is the equal-weight mean of the diagonal. The p-value comes from 10,000 random re-pairings of knockdowns with target sets. The 95% CI comes from bootstrapping TFs (5,000 resamples).
5. **Secondary statistics and checks on the primary test.**
   - **Precision-weighted mean of the diagonal.** Each TF is weighted by 1 / variance of its target set's double-centred row across knockdowns. This weight does not change under re-pairing. It stops single-gene target sets, whose diagonal values are very noisy, from dominating.
   - **Split by target count.** The diagonal was summarised separately for TFs with one target and TFs with more than one, and the test was refitted on TFs with at least 2 targets.
   - **Structural checks:**
     - a re-run without the self-exclusion;
     - the diagonal shift implied by a KD-strength × target-detection interaction;
     - the diagonal shift implied by a rank-1 interaction fitted to mismatched pairs only;
     - Spearman correlations of the per-TF values with KD strength and target detection.
6. **Spike-in sensitivity.** This asks what size of target effect the tests could detect.
   - An artificial target effect was added to the observed data, and the tests were re-run.
   - Each target of each TF was selected with probability f (0.1, 0.25, 0.5 or 1). In that TF's own knockdown only, Δ was added to |d| of every feature that lists a selected target (Δ = 0.01, 0.02 or 0.05, in Cohen's d units).
   - Percentiles and tests were then recomputed: 20 simulations per setting, 1,000 re-pairings each.
   - Δ is compared with the shift seen for the knocked-down gene's own features (step 3).
7. **Detection-matched null.** For each TF, the mean percentile of its own targets was compared with 1,000 random gene sets of the same size, matched on detection-count decile.
8. **Source-paper style Fisher test.**
   - For each TF with responding features, a one-sided Fisher test asked whether responding features are enriched for features whose top-20 list contains at least one of the TF's targets. The paper looked at the responding features' top genes; here enrichment is counted over features.
   - Results were BH-corrected across TFs.
   - Calibration: the same test was run with the 50 database TFs whose target sets are closest in size to the TF's own.
9. **GATA1 depth analysis.**
   - GATA1 cells were compared with control cells on UMI count and token count.
   - The 40 lowest-UMI `pool` controls were tested against `ref`, as a depth-only comparison.
   - The 42 GATA1 cells inside the control UMI range (at or above the control 1st percentile) were compared with 42 controls matched on log UMI (greedy nearest neighbour, 20 matchings), and with 42 random controls.
   - Null for the matched design: random control cells against UMI-matched other controls (20 draws).
10. **Units of resampling.**
    - Response tests: the cell.
    - Summaries across TFs: the TF (bootstrap).
    - Pseudo-knockdowns: the random draw.
    - Spike-ins: the simulation, with Clopper–Pearson CIs on detection rates.
    - GATA1 counts: GATA1 and `ref` cells resampled (100 bootstraps).
    - GATA1 target-set summaries: the target.

## 4. Results
**Knockdowns do change features.**
- 80.5% of knockdown TFs have at least one responding feature (95% CI 72.4–88.5%, bootstrap over TFs).
- The mean is 254 responding features per TF (CI 142–385); the median is 24 (CI 9–80).
- Pseudo-knockdowns of control cells: 6.5% of draws had any responding feature (CI 3.5–10%). The mean was 0.08 features per draw (CI 0.035–0.135), with a maximum of 4.
- After the UMI adjustment, 81.6% of TFs still respond (CI 73.6–89.7%), with a mean of 135 features (CI 69–221).

**The pipeline can see gene-specific changes (positive control, 79 TFs).**
- The knocked-down gene's mean percentile in its own knockdown is 0.760 (CI 0.690–0.826); the median is 0.943 (CI 0.747–0.986).
- 49% of TFs are above 0.95 (CI 38–61%).
- The same genes average 0.502 (CI 0.479–0.526) in the other knockdowns, a difference of +0.258 (CI 0.195–0.319).
- Features listing the knocked-down gene shift in |d| by a mean of 0.116 (CI 0.075–0.157), median 0.060 (CI 0.022–0.097), relative to other knockdowns.

**Primary analysis (union targets, 65 TFs): no positive specificity, and a small shift in the opposite direction.**
- Own targets sit at a mean response percentile of 0.452 (CI 0.403–0.501). Mismatched TF/knockdown pairs average 0.505 (CI 0.485–0.523).
- Specificity after double-centring is −0.052 on the 0–1 percentile scale, about 5 percentile points (CI −0.091 to −0.013).
  - One-sided permutation p for "own > mismatched" is 0.99.
  - Two-sided p is 0.024: own targets respond slightly *less* in their own knockdown.
- Where the shift comes from:
  - 24 single-target TFs: −0.115 (CI −0.186 to −0.045; own-target percentile 0.35; subgroup two-sided p 0.030).
  - 41 TFs with more than one target: −0.015 (CI −0.054 to 0.027; p 0.43).
  - Refit on TFs with at least 2 targets: −0.011 (CI −0.048 to 0.027), one-sided p 0.73.
- Precision-weighted statistic: −0.019 (CI −0.039 to 0.001), one-sided p 0.99, two-sided p 0.015. So a small anti-specific shift, about 2 percentile points, is also present in the larger target sets, although its bootstrap CI touches zero.
- I found no structural explanation for the shift:
  - The self-exclusion is not the cause: without it the estimate is −0.051 (CI −0.089 to −0.013).
  - A smooth KD-strength × target-detection interaction would imply +0.002 on the diagonal.
  - A rank-1 interaction fitted to the mismatched pairs accounts for −0.009, leaving −0.043.
  - Among multi-target TFs (descriptive, uncorrected), the per-TF value is lower for weaker knockdowns (Spearman ρ = 0.33, p = 0.033) and for more highly detected target sets (ρ = −0.31, p = 0.051).
  - Either way, the shift points away from specificity, not towards it.

**Sensitivity analyses.** Values are the double-centred diagonal on the 0–1 scale, with bootstrap 95% CIs over TFs and permutation p-values.

| Variant | TFs | Specificity (95% CI) | One-sided p | Two-sided p | Precision-weighted (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Union (primary) | 65 | −0.052 (−0.091 to −0.013) | 0.99 | 0.024 | −0.019 (−0.039 to 0.001) |
| TRRUST only | 58 | −0.046 (−0.096 to 0.006) | 0.95 | 0.099 | −0.036 (−0.086 to 0.008) |
| DoRothEA, all levels | 30 | −0.024 (−0.059 to 0.009) | 0.89 | 0.24 | −0.004 (−0.024 to 0.014) |
| DoRothEA A–C | 18 | +0.004 (−0.043 to 0.067) | 0.44 | 0.89 | −0.024 (−0.049 to 0.004) |
| DoRothEA ChIP-flagged | 20 | −0.005 (−0.018 to 0.008) | 0.78 | 0.43 | −0.002 (−0.011 to 0.006) |
| Union, ≥2 targets | 41 | −0.011 (−0.048 to 0.027) | 0.73 | 0.55 | −0.009 (−0.022 to 0.005) |
| Union, ≥10 targets | 22 | −0.010 (−0.025 to 0.004) | 0.93 | 0.15 | −0.003 (−0.012 to 0.004) |
| UMI-adjusted responses | 65 | −0.031 (−0.075 to 0.015) | 0.90 | 0.19 | −0.018 (−0.037 to 0.000) |
| Top-20 entries seen at ≥5 positions only | 64 | −0.046 (−0.087 to −0.008) | 0.98 | 0.036 | −0.014 (−0.033 to 0.004) |
| No self-exclusion | 65 | −0.051 (−0.089 to −0.013) | 0.99 | 0.022 | −0.019 (−0.040 to 0.001) |

- No variant gives a positive estimate whose CI excludes zero; the smallest one-sided p is 0.44.
- The anti-specific direction reaches two-sided p < 0.05 in two groups:
  - the equal-weight primary, top-20 (≥5 positions) and no-exclusion variants, all driven by single-target TFs;
  - the precision-weighted primary and UMI-adjusted statistics (p = 0.015 and 0.016).
- None of these p-values are corrected for the number of variants.

**What size of target effect could have been detected (spike-ins).**
- The detection rate is the share of 20 simulations with one-sided p < 0.05. Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs are 0.83–1 for 20/20 and 0–0.17 for 0/20.
- Δ = 0.01, 0.02 and 0.05 equal 9%, 17% and 43% of the mean |d| shift on the knocked-down gene's own features.

| Δ (d units) | Targets spiked | Percentile gain of spiked targets | Primary | Precision-weighted | ≥10 targets |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.01 | 10% | +0.09 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 0.01 | 25% | +0.08 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 0.01 | 50% | +0.07 | 0.00 | 0.95 (0.75–1.00) | 1.00 |
| 0.01 | 100% | +0.05 | 0.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0.02 | 10% | +0.17 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 0.02 | 25% | +0.15 | 0.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0.02 | 50% | +0.13 | 0.10 (0.01–0.32) | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0.02 | 100% | +0.10 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0.05 | 10% | +0.33 | 0.00 | 0.55 (0.32–0.77) | 1.00 |
| 0.05 | 25% | +0.31 | 0.45 (0.23–0.68) | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0.05 | 50% | +0.28 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0.05 | 100% | +0.22 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |

- **Multi-target tests (precision-weighted, ≥10 targets).** They would have caught a target-linked shift of about one-sixth of the direct knocked-down-gene effect on a quarter of targets, or about one-eleventh of it on half of the targets. They miss shifts of Δ ≤ 0.02 confined to 10% of targets.
- **Equal-weight primary statistic.** It is much less sensitive, because it has to overcome the noisy single-target values and the negative baseline.
- The spikes sit on top of the observed data, so detection rates are close to 0 or 1. They describe the chance over which targets are spiked, not over new cells, so they are not a classical power calculation.

**Detection-matched null.**
- Own targets average the 0.477 percentile of matched random gene sets (CI 0.399–0.556).
- 10.8% of TFs have nominal p < 0.05 (CI 3.1–18.5%), against 5% expected by chance.
- None are significant after BH correction.

**Source-paper style Fisher test (48 TFs).**
- No TF reaches q < 0.05.
- 2 TFs (4.2%, CI 0–10.4%) reach nominal p < 0.05. Size-matched wrong target sets give 6.5% (CI 4.5–8.7%).
- Ranked against those wrong target sets, own targets sit at a mean percentile of 0.51 (CI 0.44–0.57).

**GATA1: size of the response and sequencing depth.**
- **Response size.**
  - GATA1 has the largest response of any knockdown: 3,314 responding features, 67% of all features (cell bootstrap CI 3,226–3,438).
  - After the linear UMI adjustment it keeps 2,610 (CI 2,475–2,791), or 79%, and is still the largest. Among the 30 TFs with at least 100 responding features, the median TF keeps 48%.
- **GATA1 cells are much shallower than controls.**
  - Median UMI is 0.31 times that of `ref` (CI 0.29–0.35).
  - 56% of GATA1 cells (CI 45–66%) fall below the control 1st percentile of 4,781 UMI.
  - Median token count is 1,780. Only 28% of GATA1 cells reach the 2,048-token cap, against 97.5% of `ref` cells.
- **Correlation with depth sensitivity.** Across features, GATA1's response is correlated −0.71 (CI −0.73 to −0.67) with how strongly each feature tracks UMI count in control cells.
- **The linear UMI adjustment is not reliable for GATA1.**
  - It extrapolates beyond the control UMI range.
  - It over-corrects: after adjustment the response correlates +0.42 with UMI sensitivity.
  - Mean |d| falls from 0.84 to 0.65.
- **Depth alone can produce a response of this size.** The 40 lowest-UMI `pool` controls (median UMI 5,924) tested against `ref` give 3,153 responding features (CI 3,014–3,270).
- **Within the shared depth range.** The 42 GATA1 cells inside the control range (median UMI 6,482) give:
  - against UMI-matched controls (median 6,507): 430 responding features (range 415–455 over 20 matchings; mean |d| 0.29);
  - against random controls: 2,717 (range 2,430–2,918);
  - the matched-design null (control cells against UMI-matched controls): 0 in all 20 draws.
- **Reading.** Most of GATA1's response co-varies with sequencing depth, but a smaller part remains after depth matching. These data cannot tell whether GATA1 cells have lower depth for technical reasons or as a consequence of GATA1 loss (for example, loss of highly expressed erythroid transcripts).

**GATA1: target specificity.** Fisher enrichment for GATA1's own targets (exact conditional 95% CI):

| Target source | Odds ratio (95% CI) | p |
|---|---|---|
| Union (233 targets) | 1.06 (0.94–1.20) | 0.17 |
| TRRUST (11 targets) | 1.21 (0.86–1.72) | 0.15 |
| DoRothEA ChIP-flagged (219 targets) | 1.03 (0.92–1.17) | 0.30 |

- **Own-target percentiles.** Under GATA1 knockdown, GATA1's union targets sit at the 0.572 percentile (CI 0.534–0.610, bootstrap over targets), and its TRRUST targets at 0.61 (CI 0.46–0.74).
- **Comparison.** Every TF's target set averages 0.546 under GATA1 knockdown, and GATA1's targets average 0.542 under other knockdowns.
- **Specificity estimate: −0.013.** In 65% of the 65 knockdowns (including its own), GATA1's targets get a centred score at least as high as under GATA1 knockdown. The UMI-adjusted estimate is −0.010.
- **Other tests.**
  - Detection-matched percentile: 0.72 (p = 0.28).
  - Fisher p-value percentile against 50 size-matched wrong target sets: 0.82 (empirical p = 0.20).
- **Reading.** Several GATA1 metrics lean weakly positive, but none is significant. With two-thirds of all features responding, the Fisher test has little room to show enrichment, and single-TF tests have low power. There is therefore no evidence that GATA1 is a target-specific exception, but a modest GATA1-specific effect cannot be ruled out.

## 5. Verdict
**not supported.**
- Knockdowns clearly change SAE features, and the features carrying the knocked-down gene itself respond strongly.
- No test shows that responding features are tied to a TF's own targets more than to other TFs' targets, size-matched wrong target sets or detection-matched random genes. This holds across five target sources, the UMI adjustment and stricter feature–gene links. The pre-specified primary statistic even leans slightly anti-specific.
- Spike-ins show that the multi-target tests would have detected a target-linked feature shift of about one-tenth to one-sixth of the direct knocked-down-gene effect, if it reached a quarter to half of the database targets. Weaker effects, or effects confined to a small fraction of true targets, cannot be excluded.
- GATA1 follows the same pattern, and much of its large response co-varies with sequencing depth.

## 6. Limitations
- **No expression matrix.** Without one, I could not check that the database targets actually changed expression in the knockdown cells. Part of the null may come from targets that do not respond transcriptionally in K562.
- **Noisy target databases.** DoRothEA is about 88–89% level D. TRRUST sets are tiny here: 28 of 58 knocked-down TFs have a single TRRUST target, and 24 of 65 have a single union target.
- **Feature–gene links.** They come from top-20 lists built on 500 cells, and 17% of entries were seen at only one position.
- **Dilution.** Per-cell feature values average about 2,000 tokens, which dilutes gene-specific effects. Only block 5 was analysed.
- **Spike-in model.** It is simple: a uniform |d| shift on every feature that lists a target, added to the observed data. Real target effects may be uneven or show up on other features, so the detectable effect sizes are approximate.
- **Positive control.** It reflects near-complete loss of the TF's own transcript, and mostly of its token. That is far larger than a graded change in target expression, so it is used only to show that gene-specific changes are visible.
- **Unexplained anti-specific shift.** The small anti-specific shift in the primary statistic has no identified cause. It is largest for single-target TFs and also appears (−0.019) in the precision-weighted statistic. Self-exclusion and simple KD-strength × detection structure were ruled out as causes.
- **Multiplicity.** Many variants and secondary statistics were run without correcting for multiple comparisons.
- **Batch and depth.**
  - GEM-group batch was not modelled.
  - The UMI adjustment is linear and not valid for GATA1.
  - The depth-matched GATA1 comparison uses only the 42 GATA1 cells inside the control UMI range.
  - Whether GATA1's lower depth is technical or biological is unresolved.
- **Bootstrap.** The bootstrap over TFs is conditional on the fitted matrix, and TFs share targets (for example MYC), so they are not fully independent.
- **Knockdown efficiency.** It is unknown for the 7 TFs whose own gene is not measured (BRF2, FOXL2, GATA1, HINFP, HOXC10, MZF1, STAT5A). ZNRD1 is measured but is not in the gene universe, so it has no positive control.
- **Direction of change** was ignored, because |d| was used.

"""SAE knockdown-response target specificity analysis (MaxToki-217M, block-5 TopK SAE, K562 CRISPRi).
Run from the package root. Prints all reported estimates as JSON."""
import json, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import sparse
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu, rankdata, hypergeom, spearmanr, binomtest
from scipy.stats.contingency import odds_ratio
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

SEED = 20261001
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)           # core analyses
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1)      # supplementary analyses (separate stream, leaves core results unchanged)
NPERM, NBOOT, NRAND, NPSEUDO = 10000, 5000, 1000, 200
NSIM, NPERM_SIM, NBOOT_CELLS, NMATCH = 20, 1000, 100, 20

# ---------- load ----------
npz = np.load('data/cell_feature_means.npz')
man = pd.read_csv('data/cell_manifest.csv')
pos = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(npz['rows'])}
order = [pos[r] for r in man['row']]
X = npz['mean_gene'][order].astype(np.float64)
ntok = npz['n_tokens'][order]
t20 = pd.read_csv('data/feature_top20.tsv', sep='\t')
gu = pd.read_csv('data/gene_universe.tsv', sep='\t')
tr = pd.read_csv('data/targets_trrust.tsv', sep='\t')
do = pd.read_csv('data/targets_dorothea.tsv', sep='\t')
tfi = pd.read_csv('data/tf_info.tsv', sep='\t')
genes = gu.gene.values; gidx = {g: i for i, g in enumerate(genes)}
NG, F = len(genes), X.shape[1]
det = gu.detection_count.values
kdtfs = list(tfi.tf); nK = len(kdtfs)
isref = (man.group == 'ref').values; ispool = (man.group == 'pool').values; isctrl = isref | ispool
umi = man.UMI_count.values

def incidence(df):
    df = df[df.gene != '<SPECIAL>']
    G = np.zeros((F, NG)); G[df.feature_id.values, [gidx[g] for g in df.gene]] = 1
    return G
G = incidence(t20)                                         # feature x gene (top-20 membership)
G_rel = incidence(t20[t20.n_active_positions >= 5])        # only top-20 entries seen at >=5 positions
GT, GT_rel = sparse.csr_matrix(G.T), sparse.csr_matrix(G_rel.T)

t20g = t20[t20.gene != '<SPECIAL>']
data_desc = dict(
    unmeasured_tfs=tfi.tf[~tfi.tf_gene_measured.astype(bool)].tolist(),
    kd_tfs_not_in_gene_universe=[s for s in kdtfs if s not in gidx],
    n_measured=int(tfi.kd_remaining_frac.notna().sum()), n_remaining_frac_zero=int((tfi.kd_remaining_frac == 0).sum()),
    max_remaining_frac=float(tfi.kd_remaining_frac.max()),
    dorothea_level_D=int((do.confidence == 'D').sum()), dorothea_pairs=len(do),
    dorothea_level_D_kd_tfs=int((do[do.tf.isin(kdtfs)].confidence == 'D').sum()), dorothea_pairs_kd_tfs=int(do.tf.isin(kdtfs).sum()),
    trrust_kd_tfs=int(tr[tr.tf.isin(kdtfs)].tf.nunique()),
    trrust_kd_tfs_single_target=int((tr[tr.tf.isin(kdtfs)].groupby('tf').target.nunique() == 1).sum()),
    frac_top20_entries_seen_at_1_position=float(np.mean(t20g.n_active_positions == 1)),
)

# ---------- 1. responding features (KD cells vs 400 ref controls) ----------
# Adapted from the source paper (Wilcoxon test of ~20 perturbed cells vs 100K control token positions, BH FDR < 0.05,
# |effect| > 0.5): here cell-level Mann-Whitney of all KD cells vs 400 ref cells, BH across features, |Cohen d| > 0.5.
def cohen(K, R):
    n, nr = len(K), len(R)
    sp = np.sqrt((K.var(0, ddof=1) * (n - 1) + R.var(0, ddof=1) * (nr - 1)) / (n + nr - 2))
    return (K.mean(0) - R.mean(0)) / sp

def responses(XX):
    R = XX[isref]; D = np.zeros((nK, F)); Q = np.ones((nK, F))
    for i, s in enumerate(kdtfs):
        K = XX[(man.tf == s).values]
        D[i] = cohen(K, R)
        Q[i] = multipletests(mannwhitneyu(K, R, axis=0).pvalue, method='fdr_bh')[1]
    return D, Q

def n_resp(K, R):
    q = multipletests(mannwhitneyu(K, R, axis=0).pvalue, method='fdr_bh')[1]; d = cohen(K, R)
    return int(((q < 0.05) & (np.abs(d) > 0.5)).sum()), float(np.nanmean(np.abs(d)))

def pct_ci(v):
    return [float(np.percentile(v, 2.5)), float(np.percentile(v, 97.5))]

def cp_ci(k, n):
    ci = binomtest(int(k), int(n)).proportion_ci(0.95, method='exact'); return [float(ci.low), float(ci.high)]

D, Q = responses(X)
RESP = (Q < 0.05) & (np.abs(D) > 0.5)
nresp = RESP.sum(1)

lu = np.log(umi)                                           # library-size adjustment (fit in controls)
Zc = np.column_stack([np.ones(isctrl.sum()), lu[isctrl]])
B = np.linalg.lstsq(Zc, X[isctrl], rcond=None)[0]
X_umi = X - np.outer(lu, B[1])
D_umi, Q_umi = responses(X_umi)
RESP_umi = (Q_umi < 0.05) & (np.abs(D_umi) > 0.5)
nresp_umi = RESP_umi.sum(1)
gi = kdtfs.index('GATA1'); isg = (man.tf == 'GATA1').values
Xu_g, Xu_r = X_umi[isg], X_umi[isref]
del X_umi

pool_idx = np.where(ispool)[0]; sizes = tfi.n_kd_cells.values   # pseudo-knockdowns from pool controls
pseudo = []
for b in range(NPSEUDO):
    idx = rng.choice(pool_idx, rng.choice(sizes), replace=False)
    q = multipletests(mannwhitneyu(X[idx], X[isref], axis=0).pvalue, method='fdr_bh')[1]
    pseudo.append(int(((q < 0.05) & (np.abs(cohen(X[idx], X[isref])) > 0.5)).sum()))

def pct_row(A, s, G, GT, exclude_self=True):

# Permutation null: random re-pairing of KDs with target sets (column permutation; dcenter commutes with it).
# Secondary statistic: precision-weighted mean of the diagonal, weight = 1 / variance of the target set's
# double-centred row across KDs (unchanged by re-pairing), so single-gene sets no longer dominate.
def specificity(P, pairs, min_targets=1, r=None):

    n = len(tfl); M = buildM(P, ts, tfl)

    perms = np.array([r.permutation(n) for _ in range(NPERM)])
    Z = DC[np.arange(n)[None, :], perms]                     # re-paired diagonals
    null = np.nanmean(Z, 1)

               p_greater=float((np.sum(null >= obs) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)),
               p_two_sided=float((np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)),
               own_mean_pct=float(np.nanmean(np.diag(M))), own_mean_pct_ci=boot_ci(np.diag(M), r=r),
               mismatched_mean_pct=float(np.nanmean(M[~np.eye(n, dtype=bool)])))

    res['mismatched_mean_pct_ci'] = boot_ci(np.array([np.nanmean(M[k, off[k]]) for k in range(n)]), r=rng2)
    w = 1 / np.nanvar(DC, 1); obs_w = float(wmean(I, w)); null_w = wmean(Z, w)

    ntg = np.array([np.sum(~np.isnan(P[kdtfs.index(s), ts[s]])) for s in tfl])
